analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on payday lenders, online loan lead-sellers, and overdraft fees on prepaid cards.
analysis.headline: The SAFE Lending Act drew 13 cosponsors in the Senate, but the Banking Committee never took it up and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten rules on small-dollar, high-cost lending. It would require small-dollar lenders to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, make online and national-bank small-dollar loans follow the interest-rate and fee laws of the borrower's home state, and stop middlemen from collecting and selling borrowers' Social Security and bank account numbers without actually making the loan. It would also ban overdraft fees on prepaid cards and give consumers more control over payments pulled from their bank accounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income borrowers who use payday loans, installment loans, and prepaid cards. They would gain the right to stop automatic electronic repayments, keep remote checks from draining their accounts without written consent, and rely on their own state's rate caps even when the loan comes from an out-of-state website or a national bank.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small-dollar borrowers and prepaid card users

how_it_helps.text: A remotely created check — a check the borrower never signed — could only be issued by a person the consumer designated in writing, with the designation given directly to the consumer's bank, and the consumer could revoke it at any time.
If a borrower agrees to repay a small-dollar loan by electronic fund transfer, that transfer is treated like a preauthorized transfer, which carries protections including the right to stop payment.

Small-dollar lenders (loans of $5,000 or less, repaid within about 12 months) must register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau before issuing credit, and brokering or arranging such loans counts too.

Small-dollar loans made over the internet, by phone, by mail, or by a national bank must comply with the rate and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives — closing the channel that lets online lenders and bank partners charge rates a state has banned.
Overdraft fees on prepaid accounts are prohibited, and a transaction that exceeds the prepaid balance can still be declined but the consumer cannot be charged for it.

Lead generators — websites that collect a borrower's Social Security number or bank account details and sell them to lenders — must be the ones actually making the loan; pure middlemen may no longer traffic in that sensitive information.
The Government Accountability Office would study small-dollar credit on Indian reservations and its effect on economic opportunity for tribal members.

analysis.who_pays: Payday and online installment lenders, lead-generation websites that sell loan applications, and prepaid card issuers that collect overdraft fees. They would lose fee income and, for lenders relying on out-of-state rate structures, their ability to charge rates the borrower's own state has outlawed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders, lead sellers, prepaid issuers

drawbacks.text: Requiring registration and applying state rate caps to online and national-bank small-dollar loans would push some lenders out of the market or out of lending to riskier borrowers, which industry and some economists argue would leave the people who use these loans with fewer options when banks will not lend to them.

The written-designation rule for remotely created checks and the restrictions on selling loan-application data would add compliance costs for legitimate payment processors and comparison-shopping websites, not only fraudulent operators.
The bill relies on Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rulemaking within a year of enactment, so the actual shape and timing of the protections would depend on the bureau of the day.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go directly to borrowers who are disproportionately low-income: stopping unauthorized account withdrawals, ending prepaid overdraft fees, and forcing online lenders to obey state rate caps address well-documented harms of small-dollar lending. The real trade-off is access — if high-rate lenders cannot operate profitably, some borrowers may lose a last-resort (if expensive) source of cash or turn to informal lenders. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how many borrowers are trapped by fee cycles versus how many genuinely rely on these loans.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-November 2022 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which took no action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on November 16, 2022, joined by 13 cosponsors — 12 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
That referral was the bill's only action; the committee never held a hearing or markup, and the chamber never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday and online small-dollar lenders, loan-application lead sellers, and prepaid card issuers are better off: none of the restrictions took effect, so they keep their existing fee income and their ability to make loans under out-of-state rate rules. Borrowers gain nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Payday lenders, lead sellers, prepaid issuers

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SAFE Lending Act of 2022 in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown (D)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Offered no support; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and the measure never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 senators behind the bill were Democrats or the chamber's Independents — 12 of 48 Senate Democrats, 1 of 2 Independents, and the Democratic sponsor — and no Republican signed on; the bill never came to a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would force these lenders to register with the CFPB and, for loans made online or through national banks, obey the rate and fee laws of the borrower's home state — eliminating the channel by which lenders charge rates a state has banned. Borrowers' gain is these lenders' lost fee and interest income.

Websites that collect and sell applicants' Social Security and bank account numbers without making loans themselves would be barred from the business; the bill lets only actual lenders handle that sensitive data.
Overdraft fees on prepaid accounts would be banned, ending a fee stream charged largely to consumers who use prepaid cards in place of bank accounts.

industries.industry: Payment processors and banks handling remotely created checks
industries.note: Checks drawn without the account holder's signature could only be issued with a written designation on file at the consumer's bank, cutting off a common fraud and unauthorized-withdrawal channel but adding verification steps for legitimate users.
